answer.rationale: The strongest signal is temporal: the release landed 2 hours ago and write-path p99 has been climbing for 90 minutes, which fits a post-deploy regression that took a few minutes to manifest under load. Rollback (memory_b1) is the one candidate that is both causally aimed at the most likely trigger and reversible; if it is wrong, we have lost a window but not customer writes. Regional failover (memory_b2) is superficially attractive because the degradation is confined to the primary region, but region-confinement is exactly what a staged/canary-gated release would look like if the new build is only live in one region, so 'confined to one region' is not evidence for an infrastructure-level regional fault. Failover during the settlement peak with heavy writes is the single highest-risk option against the primary objective of not losing customer writes: in-flight writes and replication lag at peak are where write loss actually happens. Capacity (memory_b3) worked when provisioned ahead of a known surge, not as a 90-minute-in remedy, and it would only mask a code-level regression. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) fit a failing external dependency, which is not what we are seeing. Read-replica routing (memory_b5) helped when dashboard reads were starving the primary; there is no reported read-load signal here, only heavy writes. I want to verify memory_b1 because it is the memory my action rests on, and the consolidated one-line summary hides the things that decide whether it transfers: was that rollback done at traffic peak or in a quiet window, was the schema/migration surface comparable, and how long did the rollback actually take to propagate. 'Finished without customer impact' at day 18 may simply mean it was done at low volume. Note the survivorship problem in this whole memory set: every inherited record is a success story, so it encodes which interventions were tried and worked, not their base rates or the cases where they made things worse. That biases me toward pattern-matching rather than diagnosing. Therefore I am scoping this as a guarded partial rollback: revert the canary/lowest-share cohort of the primary region first, hold 10-15 minutes, and confirm write p99 bends before widening. If p99 does not respond, the release is exonerated and regional failover becomes the next-window candidate with an explicit write-drain plan. Concrete risk to flag downstream: a rollback executed at settlement peak can itself drop or duplicate in-flight writes if the prior build's write path is not fully compatible, so this must go out with idempotency keys honored and drain-before-cut, not as a hard cut. I also want the reversal decision and the outcome recorded either way, so the next session inherits the negative result too, not just another success line.
